lead: A resistor opposes current at every frequency. Inductors and capacitors oppose AC by amounts that change with frequency and shift current in time against voltage. As complex numbers all three form impedance Z. Then I = V/Z gives current size and phase. Fan regulators, tube-light chokes and power-factor capacitors use this analysis.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.3 for phasors and the j-operator, and Unit 1 for resistance, series circuits and Ohm's law.

blocks.text: Inductive reactance X<sub>L</sub> is opposition from an inductor. It grows with frequency because faster current changes induce larger back emf.

blocks.where: X<sub>L</sub> is inductive reactance in ohm (Ω); ω is angular frequency in rad/s; f is frequency in hertz (Hz); L is inductance in henry (H).

blocks.text: Capacitive reactance X<sub>C</sub> falls as frequency rises; the capacitor has less time to charge before supply reverses.

blocks.where: X<sub>C</sub> is capacitive reactance in Ω; C is capacitance in farad (F).

blocks.text: Reactance is magnitude only; phase is separate. Voltage across L leads current by 90°, so Z<sub>L</sub> = jX<sub>L</sub>. Voltage across C lags by 90°, so Z<sub>C</sub> = −jX<sub>C</sub>.
R and net reactance are 90° apart and combine like right-triangle legs.
Z = R + jX = R + j(X<sub>L</sub> − X<sub>C</sub>),   |Z| = √(R² + X²),   φ = tan⁻¹(X/R)
blocks.where: Z is impedance in Ω; R is resistance in Ω; X is net reactance X<sub>L</sub> − X<sub>C</sub> in Ω; |Z| is magnitude in Ω; φ is angle of Z in degrees, positive when X<sub>L</sub> > X<sub>C</sub>.

blocks.text: Admittance Y = 1/Z = G + jB, in siemens (S). Parallel branches use Y because branch admittances add.
In series, same current flows. Take current as reference at 0°; supply voltage is phasor sum of element voltages.

items: X<sub>L</sub> = ωL and X<sub>C</sub> = 1/(ωC) in Ω.
I = V/Z; magnitude V/|Z| in ampere (A).
V<sub>R</sub> = IR, V<sub>L</sub> = IX<sub>L</sub>, V<sub>C</sub> = IX<sub>C</sub> in volt (V).
φ = tan⁻¹(X/R); state lead or lag.

blocks.text: R-L: X<sub>C</sub> = 0, X positive, current lags; fan motor near no load. R-C: X<sub>L</sub> = 0, X negative, current leads; capacitor-run fan.
Element voltages do not add as plain numbers; they form a right triangle with base V<sub>R</sub> and height V<sub>L</sub> − V<sub>C</sub>.

blocks.where: V is RMS supply voltage in V; V<sub>R</sub>, V<sub>L</sub>, V<sub>C</sub> are RMS element voltages in V.

blocks.text: In series R-L-C, X<sub>L</sub> and X<sub>C</sub> have opposite phase effects. Net reactance is their difference.
Last row is series resonance: current limited by R alone and largest. Some syllabi treat resonance separately; sign of X gives the behaviour.

V<sub>L</sub> or V<sub>C</sub> can exceed supply voltage. Kirchhoff's law holds: the two are nearly opposite in phase, so phasors partly cancel. A 230 V supply can hold 332 V across a capacitor, so rating matters.
In parallel, each branch sees full supply voltage. Convert each branch to admittance, add, then divide once.

blocks.where: I is total RMS current in A; V is RMS supply voltage in V; Y is total admittance in S; Y₁, Y₂ are branch admittances in S.

items: Resistor branch: Y = 1/R, real and positive.

blocks.text: Conductances add; susceptances add with signs. Sign of total susceptance decides lead or lag. A capacitor across a motor winding corrects power factor.

figure.caption: From given values to answer: reactances, net reactance, impedance, current, angle. Negative X gives negative φ and leading current.

spec.title: Series RLC solution steps
spec.aria: Flow from R, L and C values to reactance, net reactance, impedance, current and phase angle.

examples.question: A series circuit has R = 30 Ω, L = 0.1 H and C = 50 μF, across v = 230√2 sin(314t) V. Find X<sub>L</sub>, X<sub>C</sub>, impedance, RMS current, phase angle (leading or lagging) and RMS voltage across each element.
steps: v = 230√2 sin(314t) V gives V = 230 V rms and ω = 314 rad/s (50 Hz).
examples.answer: Z = 44.1 Ω at −47.1° (capacitive), I = 5.22 A rms leading by 47.1°, with V<sub>R</sub> = 156.5 V, V<sub>L</sub> = 163.8 V and V<sub>C</sub> = 332.4 V.
examples.check:
import math
R, L, C, w, V = 30.0, 0.1, 50e-6, 314.0, 230.0
XL = w * L
XC = 1 / (w * C)
X = XL - XC
Z = math.hypot(R, X)
I = V / Z
phi = math.degrees(math.atan2(X, R))
print(round(XL, 1))
print(round(XC, 1))
print(round(X, 1))
print(round(Z, 1))
print(round(I, 2))
print(round(phi, 1))
print(round(I * R, 1))
print(round(I * XL, 1))
print(round(I * XC, 1))

traps: Adding R, X<sub>L</sub> and X<sub>C</sub> arithmetically. Combine X<sub>L</sub> with X<sub>C</sub> first, then use √(R² + X²).
Using f where ω is needed. X<sub>L</sub> = 2πfL, not fL.
Forgetting X<sub>C</sub> is a magnitude. The capacitor contributes −jX<sub>C</sub>, so it subtracts from X<sub>L</sub>.
Reporting φ as current angle alone. φ = tan⁻¹(X/R) is angle of Z, equal to (angle of V) − (angle of I).
Assuming each element voltage must be below supply voltage. In series R-L-C, V<sub>L</sub> or V<sub>C</sub> can exceed V.

quiz.q: Write formulas for X<sub>L</sub> and X<sub>C</sub>, with unit of each symbol.
quiz.a: X<sub>L</sub> = ωL = 2πfL in Ω, with ω in rad/s, f in Hz, L in H. X<sub>C</sub> = 1/(ωC) = 1/(2πfC) in Ω, with C in F.

quiz.q: Why does current lag in R-L but lead in R-C?
quiz.a: An inductor opposes current change, so its current rises after voltage; series current lags. Capacitor current depends on rate of change of voltage, so it peaks before voltage; series current leads.

quiz.q: A 100 Ω resistor is in series with a 0.2 H inductor across 50 Hz. Find |Z| and φ.
R = 20 Ω, X<sub>L</sub> = 60 Ω and X<sub>C</sub> = 30 Ω are in series across 200 V rms. Find RMS current and capacitor voltage.
In series R-L-C, current is in phase with supply and largest. What does this tell about X<sub>L</sub>, X<sub>C</sub> and element voltages?
quiz.a: In-phase current means X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>, so net reactance is zero, Z = R and I = V/R is maximum. V<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>C</sub> are equal and opposite, so they cancel; each can exceed supply voltage.

quiz.q: What is admittance, its unit, and why is it convenient for parallel circuits?
quiz.a: Admittance Y = 1/Z, in siemens (S). Branch admittances add directly in parallel, so one addition and I = V·Y give total current.

quiz.q: A series R-L and a series R-C have same |Z| and same RMS supply. Compare their currents.
quiz.a: Current magnitudes are equal, I = V/|Z|. Phases differ: R-L current lags by φ and R-C current leads by φ, where |φ| = cos⁻¹(R/|Z|) is same for both; currents are mirror images about voltage phasor.

beyond: Not for the exam. Power engineers use this complex arithmetic in load-flow software for state grids. Phasor measurement units report phase angle live from a substation. Filter designers use the impedance divider for audio crossovers and EMI filters.
